title: Why a Ship Needs Marine Insurance, and How Hull and Cargo Claims Are Made
canonical_question: Why does a ship require marine insurance cover? Explain hull claims and cargo claims in marine insurance. State the documents and information required from the ship in support of such claims, and indicate their validity.
present_day_examinable_core: Three tasks in one question, and the third is the one that separates candidates. Establish WHY cover exists - indemnity, compulsion by convention and contract, and financeability of trade. Then distinguish a HULL claim (the owner's own property loss, on his own policy) from a CARGO claim (which reaches the ship as a LIABILITY under the contract of carriage, and is therefore P&I rather than hull). Then produce the ship's evidence pack and say what makes each item good - which is a Chief Engineer's actual job in a claim, and the part a candidate can be asked to do on the day.

recommended_exam_depth.note: MIW's recommendation for a whole-question answer of three parts. The sittings that evidence this family print a paper total only, with no per-question split, so no mark here is inherited from any examiner's paper.

understand_first: The single mistake that costs most marks here is treating 'cargo claim' as one thing. It is two, and they sit on opposite sides of the ship. When cargo is damaged, the cargo owner claims on HIS OWN cargo policy - that is a cargo underwriter paying his own assured, and the ship is not a party to it. What then reaches the ship is the cargo underwriter's SUBROGATED claim against the carrier under the bill of lading. That is a third-party liability, so it is met by the P&I club and not by the hull and machinery policy. A candidate who writes that 'cargo claims are settled under the H&M policy' has said something structurally wrong about the whole market, and no amount of correct detail afterwards recovers it. The second thing to hold onto is that insurance is a contract of INDEMNITY resting on utmost good faith: it puts the assured back where he was, no better, and it can be defeated by what the ship failed to disclose, failed to maintain or failed to document. That is why the third part of this question - the documents and their validity - is not administrative padding. It is the part that decides whether the claim is paid.

blocks.h: Three headed parts, in the examiner's own order

blocks.p: Head the answer Why cover is required, Hull claims, Cargo claims, Documents and their validity. The last part is worth real marks and is the one most often left as a hurried list, so give it a table and give each document a reason.

ul: Why - three reasons, not one: indemnity against a loss no owner can absorb; compulsion by convention and by contract; and the fact that no bank, charterer or shipper will deal with an uninsured ship.

Hull - name the policy (Institute Time Clauses Hulls, or the International Hull Clauses), then the claim types: particular average, general average contribution, salvage, sue and labour, collision liability, unrepaired damage, constructive and actual total loss - and the deductible.
Cargo - draw the two-sided distinction above explicitly. Then the carrier's duties and defences under the carriage regime, the package/weight limitation, and the one-year time bar.

Documents - group them (statutory, class, operational, cargo, financial), and against each say what it proves and what makes it valid. State that the ship's certificates matter because cover is contingent on class and on seaworthiness.
Say 'no survey, no claim'. Damage repaired before the underwriter's surveyor has seen it is the commonest way a good claim is lost.

blocks.h: 1. Why a ship requires marine insurance cover

blocks.p: Marine insurance is a contract of indemnity: for a premium, the insurer agrees to put the assured back into the position he was in before an insured loss. In India the contract is governed by the Marine Insurance Act 1963, which codifies the doctrines the whole market runs on - insurable interest, utmost good faith and the duty of disclosure, warranties, the classes of loss, general average, sue and labour, and subrogation. Three separate reasons make cover necessary rather than prudent.

ul: The exposure is larger than the asset. A single casualty can produce a total loss of the ship, wreck removal, a pollution liability, cargo liability, salvage and third-party property damage at once. No shipowner can carry that on his balance sheet, and it is uninsurable exposure - not the day-to-day maintenance bill - that the market exists to absorb.

Compulsion by convention. A ship cannot trade without evidence of financial security in several regimes: the CLC 1992 certificate for oil pollution from a laden tanker, the Bunkers Convention 2001 certificate for bunker oil pollution, the Nairobi Wreck Removal Convention 2007 certificate, the passenger liability certificate under the Athens Convention as amended by the 2002 Protocol, and the MLC 2006 financial security for repatriation and for death or long-term disability. These are carried certificates, they are inspected at port State control, and they are all evidence of insurance.

Compulsion by contract. The mortgagee bank requires hull cover assigned to it; the charterparty requires the ship to be entered with a club and classed with an IACS society; the shipper's letter of credit assumes a documented, insured carriage. Cover is what makes the ship a tradeable and financeable asset.

blocks.p: The practical division of the market follows the risk. Hull and machinery insures the owner's own property. Protection and indemnity, written by mutual clubs, insures his liabilities to other people - cargo, crew, pollution, wreck, collision liability beyond the hull policy's share. Loss of hire insures earnings. Cargo insurance belongs to the cargo interest and not to the ship at all. Knowing which policy answers a given loss is the skill this question is testing.

A hull claim is made by the owner on his own hull and machinery policy, which in practice is written on the Institute Time Clauses Hulls or on the International Hull Clauses 2003. The ship is insured for an agreed value, each accident carries a deductible, and the policy responds only to the perils it names.

headers: The point that earns the mark
rows: Particular average
Accidental partial damage to the ship itself, borne by the ship's own interest
The ordinary hull claim - grounding, heavy weather, machinery damage from an insured peril
General average contribution
The ship's share of a sacrifice or extraordinary expenditure made for the common safety
Adjusted under the York-Antwerp Rules by an average adjuster, and recovered from the hull policy. GA is a division of loss between ship, cargo and freight; the hull policy pays the ship's share of it
Salvage and salvage charges
The salvage award or contractual remuneration
Whether it is a GA item or a particular charge depends on whether the service was for the common safety
Sue and labour
Reasonable expense the assured incurs to avert or minimise an insured loss
Payable in addition to the loss, and it is the clause that rewards the Chief Engineer who acts. Doing nothing to limit damage is itself a breach
Collision liability
The ship's liability to the other vessel following a collision

The hull policy carries a stated proportion of it - three-fourths under the traditional running down clause - and the balance, together with liabilities the clause excludes such as pollution, wreck removal and cargo, falls on P&I
Unrepaired damage
Insured damage not repaired before the policy ends or before sale
Measured by the reasonable depreciation in the ship's market value, capped at the cost of repair
Constructive total loss
The ship is not destroyed but recovery or repair would cost more than the insured value
The assured must give notice of abandonment to claim as for a total loss
Actual total loss
The ship is destroyed, or so damaged that it is no longer the thing insured, or is missing
No notice of abandonment is needed

blocks.p: How a hull claim is actually run. The sequence is what a Chief Engineer is examined on, and it is unforgiving of the wrong order:

ol: Act to limit the damage, and record what was done and when - that is the sue and labour duty and it is also the best evidence of good seamanship.
Notify at once - the Company and DPA, the classification society where class is affected, and the underwriters through the broker. Note protest where a peril of the seas or a third party is involved.

Survey before repair. The underwriter's surveyor and the class surveyor attend, damage is examined, measured and photographed in the found condition, and the cause is recorded. Repairing first and claiming afterwards is the commonest way a valid claim is lost, because the extent and cause can no longer be proved.

Repair specification and competitive quotations, submitted for the underwriter's approval, with the repair carried out by an approved repairer under class attendance and the damage repairs separated from owner's work on the yard account. An unsplit dry-dock invoice invites a dispute over every line of it.
Claim submission - the survey report, invoices, log extracts and the cause statement - and where general average or a collision is involved, adjustment by an average adjuster.
Settlement, less the deductible, and the insurer is then subrogated to the owner's rights against any third party responsible.

blocks.p: What defeats a hull claim. Ordinary wear and tear, gradual deterioration and inherent vice are excluded, because the policy is not a maintenance contract. Beyond that, the classification clause requires the ship to be in class with an approved society and the class maintained, with recommendations and conditions of class discharged within their dates; unseaworthiness with the owner's privity, want of due diligence, breach of an express warranty, non-disclosure of a material fact, and unreasonable delay in notification all give the underwriter a defence. Every one of those is an evidential question - which is what part three of this question is about.

blocks.h: 3. Cargo claims - and which side of the ship they land on

blocks.p: Two different claims share the name, and the distinction is the heart of this part.

ul: The cargo owner's claim on his own cargo policy. Cargo is insured by the cargo interest, in the London market normally on the Institute Cargo Clauses (A), (B) or (C) - (A) being the widest all-risks cover, (B) and (C) named-perils cover of decreasing scope. All three respond to a general average contribution. The ship is not a party to this contract and does not defend it.

The subrogated claim against the ship. Having paid its assured, the cargo underwriter steps into the cargo owner's shoes and sues the carrier under the contract of carriage evidenced by the bill of lading. To the shipowner this is a third-party liability, and it is answered by the P&I club, not by the hull policy.

blocks.p: The carriage regime, and the Indian statute book is new. The governing statutes are the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 2025 (Act 19 of 2025), whose Schedule carries the carriage regime, and the Bills of Lading Act, 2025 (Act 18 of 2025), which governs the transfer of rights and liabilities under the bill and therefore who may sue. Both came into force on 10 September 2025, repealing the Indian Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1925 and the Indian Bills of Lading Act 1856 respectively. A candidate citing the 1925 or 1856 Acts as current Indian law is citing repealed statutes.

Under the Schedule the carrier must exercise due diligence - not an absolute duty, and not a continuing one - to make the ship seaworthy, properly man, equip and supply her, and make the holds and other cargo spaces fit and safe for the reception, carriage and preservation of the goods before and at the beginning of the voyage; and must properly and carefully load, handle, stow, carry, keep, care for and discharge the goods. Against that stand the carrier's defences - among them error in the navigation or management of the ship, fire without the carrier's actual fault or privity, perils of the sea, inherent vice, insufficiency of packing and latent defect not discoverable by due diligence - together with a limitation of 666.67 units of account per package or unit, or 2 units of account per kilogramme of gross weight, whichever is the higher, and a one-year time bar. Any clause lessening the carrier's liability below the Schedule is void.

And the Indian Schedule is not Hague-Visby renumbered. It enacts the Hague Rules as amended with modifications, and three of the departures are worth marks. "Goods" INCLUDES live animals and cargo carried on or under deck, which Hague-Visby excludes - so the familiar sentence "deck cargo and live animals are outside the rules" is false in India. The one-year time bar may be extended by three months by the court. And Article IV bis is not in the Schedule, so the tidy proposition that the carrier's defences and limits apply equally in tort and extend to servants and agents cannot be asserted from the Indian text. Answer from the Indian Schedule, not from the international instrument.

What the ship does about a cargo claim. Prevent it where possible and document it where not: reject or clause a bill of lading that does not describe the goods as they were received, never sign a clean bill against a letter of indemnity for cargo known to be damaged, tally and record apparent order and condition, keep the ventilation, temperature, bilge-sounding and hold-cleaning records that answer the usual allegations, hold hatch covers weathertight and keep the ultrasonic test report, attend a joint survey with the claimant's surveyor at discharge, and issue a letter of protest where the cargo's condition or the shore handling is the cause. Notify the club early: the club appoints the correspondent and the surveyor, and its cover assumes it was told in time.

blocks.h: 4. The documents and information required from the ship, and their validity

blocks.p: The ship is the only source for most of this, and a claim is built from it. Two different senses of validity matter, and both should be stated. A record is valid if it is contemporaneous, complete and unaltered; a certificate is valid if it is in date and properly endorsed.

rows: Deck and engine log books, movement book, engine data logger and alarm printouts
The sequence of events, the weather, the machinery's condition and what the watch actually did
Contemporaneous entries in the official log, unaltered, signed; retained for the period the flag State and the Company require
Note of protest / letter of protest, and statement of facts
That the master reserved the owner's position against a peril or a third party
Noted before a competent authority promptly on arrival, and normally before breaking bulk, with an extended protest reserved if the full extent is not yet known
Master's and Chief Engineer's damage report, ISM non-conformity, accident and near-miss reports, investigation report
Cause, extent, immediate action taken - and the sue and labour effort
Raised in the SMS and reported to the DPA at the time; a report written weeks later is worth a fraction of one written on the day
VDR and course recorder data, ECDIS and AIS records, engine telegraph log
The independent record of a collision, grounding or manoeuvring casualty
Only valid if secured immediately: the VDR record is overwritten on a rolling basis, so it must be saved and downloaded before it is lost
Survey reports - underwriter's surveyor, class surveyor, joint survey with the claimant, independent expert
The damage as found, and the opinion on cause
Damage examined before repair, in the presence of the parties, with photographs and measurements; an unwitnessed survey is arguable
Repair specification, competitive quotations, yard invoices, dry-dock account, spares and stores invoices, towage and port disbursements
The quantum of the claim
Damage work separated from owner's work; the underwriter's approval obtained before the work rather than after it
Certificate of Class, survey status report, outstanding recommendations and conditions of class, machinery survey (including continuous survey) records
That the classification warranty was kept
Class in force, periodical surveys not overdue, and every recommendation and condition of class discharged within its date. A single overdue item is the underwriter's easiest defence

Statutory certificates - Cargo Ship Safety Construction, Equipment and Radio (or the Safety Certificate), International Load Line, IOPP, IAPP, IEE, Sewage, ISM DOC and SMC, ISSC, MLC Certificate and DMLC, Tonnage, Continuous Synopsis Record
Seaworthiness in the documentary sense, and compliance with the conventions

Generally a five-year certificate kept alive by annual and intermediate surveys and the resulting endorsements. Tonnage and the CSR are not periodical in the same way. An expired or unendorsed certificate is evidence of unseaworthiness and can breach the policy
Insurance and financial-security certificates - CLC, Bunkers, Wreck Removal, passenger liability, MLC financial security; club certificate of entry
That the compulsory cover was in place at the time of the incident
In force at the date of the casualty, matching the ship's particulars, and issued for the correct trade
Crew documents - certificates of competency and endorsements, Minimum Safe Manning Document, records of hours of work and rest, familiarisation and drill records, medical certificates
That the ship was properly manned, which is a seaworthiness question and a defence-destroying one if it fails
Certificates in date and endorsed by the flag State; rest-hour records complete and matching the watch system actually worked

Cargo documents - bill of lading and its clausing, mate's receipt, manifest, stowage and lashing plan, tally sheets, draught or ullage survey, temperature and ventilation logs, hold cleanliness and hatch cover ultrasonic test reports, letters of protest
The apparent order and condition on receipt, and the care given during carriage
Signed by the party who checked the goods, dated, and consistent with the log. A clean bill signed against a letter of indemnity for cargo known to be damaged destroys the club's cover for that claim
General average documents - the adjuster's statement, GA bond and GA guarantee, valuations, and the accounts of the sacrifice or expenditure
The apportionment between ship, cargo and freight
Security collected from cargo interests before delivery, since after delivery there is nothing to hold
Pollution and bunker records - Oil Record Books Parts I and II, bunker delivery notes and retained samples, garbage and ballast water records
That an environmental allegation can be answered
Entries current and signed; the retained bunker sample kept for the period required and properly sealed and labelled

blocks.p: The time limits are part of validity. Notice of the casualty is due under the policy without unreasonable delay; a note of protest is normally taken before breaking bulk; a cargo claim against the carrier is barred one year after delivery; notice of abandonment must be given to claim a constructive total loss; and general average security must be taken before the cargo leaves the ship. A perfect evidence pack produced after the bar has run is worth nothing, and that is the honest summary of this part of the question.

The examiner has asked three distinct things and the marks are split between them, so an answer that spends fourteen marks' worth of writing on hull claims and two lines on documents cannot score well however good the fourteen are. The document part also rewards the one thing a candidate genuinely knows better than a lawyer does: which records exist on a ship, who holds them, and how quickly they stop being usable.

ul: Putting cargo claims on the hull policy. Cargo damage reaches the shipowner as a liability under the bill of lading and is met by P&I. Say so explicitly - it is a discriminating point and it is easy marks.

Confusing general average with particular average. Particular average is accidental partial damage borne by the interest that suffered it. General average is a deliberate sacrifice or extraordinary expenditure for the common safety, shared between ship, cargo and freight, and adjusted under the York-Antwerp Rules.

Forgetting the classification warranty. Candidates treat class and insurance as separate subjects. They are joined: the policy requires class to be maintained, so an overdue survey or an undischarged condition of class is an insurance problem as much as a statutory one.

blocks.h: What this answer deliberately does not claim

ul: No section numbers from the Marine Insurance Act 1963. The Act is named as the governing Indian statute and its doctrines are stated, because those are what the question needs. Section numbers are not quoted, since MIW has not read the Gazette text for this entry and a mis-cited section is worse in an answer script than no section at all.

The Indian carriage position is stated from MIW's own primary reading, not from the international instrument. Both 2025 Acts were read at source in the Gazette of India during MIW's verification of the solved QP2510 Q2 - the Bills of Lading Act 2025 as Act 18 of 2025 and the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 2025 as Act 19 of 2025, including the entire Schedule - and their commencement on 10 September 2025 is established from the notifications S.O. 4083(E) and S.O. 4082(E) of 8 September 2025. That is why this entry states the Indian departures from Hague-Visby rather than treating the Schedule as Hague-Visby by another name: relying on 'the content common to both' would have carried the deck-cargo exclusion into an answer where it is false.

The package and weight limitation IS given, because MIW read it in the Indian Schedule - 666.67 units of account per package or unit, or 2 per kilogramme, whichever is higher. No monetary limit is given for any of the liability conventions, and none should be: those are unit-of-account figures which are periodically raised, no rupee conversion is asserted anywhere, and quoting a stale one is a false claim about current law.

blocks.h: Where the solved corpus takes this further

blocks.p: MIW's solved papers already answer several neighbouring tasks in more depth than this entry does, and they are worth reading beside it: the types of marine insurance policy and their exclusions, P&I compared with H&M, the running down clause with general average expenses and a claim for unrepaired damage, and general average under the York-Antwerp Rules. None of them answers THIS question - none states the documents required from the ship and their validity - which is why this entry exists. But they are the deeper treatment of the parts they do cover.

quick_revision.recall_15s: Cover exists for three reasons: the exposure exceeds the asset, conventions compel it (CLC, Bunkers, Wreck Removal, passenger, MLC financial security), and no bank or charterer deals with an uninsured ship. Hull claims are the owner's own property on the H&M policy - particular average, GA contribution, salvage, sue and labour, collision liability, unrepaired damage, CTL with notice of abandonment, ATL - less a deductible. Cargo claims are two things: the cargo owner on his own ICC (A)/(B)/(C) policy, then the subrogated claim against the carrier under the bill of lading, which is P&I. Survey before repair, split damage from owner's work, keep class alive, and produce a contemporaneous evidence pack before the time bars run.
keywords: insurable interest and utmost good faith
critical_numbers: One year - the time bar on a cargo claim against the carrier, running from delivery or from the date of intended delivery
Three-fourths - the proportion of collision liability traditionally carried by the hull policy under the running down clause, the remaining fourth and the excluded liabilities falling on P&I
Five years - the normal life of a statutory certificate, kept alive by annual and intermediate surveys and their endorsements

10 September 2025 - the date BOTH the Bills of Lading Act 2025 (Act 18 of 2025) and the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 2025 (Act 19 of 2025) came into force, vide S.O. 4083(E) and S.O. 4082(E) of 8 September 2025, repealing the Indian Bills of Lading Act 1856 and the Indian Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1925

666.67 units of account per package or unit, or 2 per kilogramme of gross weight, whichever is the higher - the carrier's limitation under the Schedule to the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 2025. No rupee conversion is asserted
Three months - the further period by which a court may extend the one-year time bar under the Indian Schedule. This is one of the four respects in which the Indian Schedule departs from Hague-Visby
quick_revision.critical_regulation: Marine Insurance Act 1963 (India) for the contract itself - indemnity, insurable interest, utmost good faith and disclosure, warranties, classes of loss, general average, sue and labour, subrogation. Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 2025 (Act 19 of 2025), whose Schedule carries the carriage regime, and the Bills of Lading Act, 2025 (Act 18 of 2025) for transfer of rights and title to sue - BOTH in force from 10 September 2025, and the Schedule enacts the Hague Rules as amended WITH MODIFICATIONS. Compulsory financial security under CLC 1992, the Bunkers Convention 2001, the Nairobi Wreck Removal Convention 2007, the Athens Convention as amended by the 2002 Protocol, and MLC 2006. Policy wordings - Institute Time Clauses Hulls or International Hull Clauses 2003 for the ship; Institute Cargo Clauses (A), (B), (C) for cargo - are MARKET documents, not law, and should be named as such.
quick_revision.major_trap: Saying that cargo claims are settled under the ship's hull and machinery policy. They are not: cargo reaches the ship as a liability under the bill of lading and is answered by the P&I club.

authority_sources.source: Marine Insurance Act 1963 (India) - the governing statute for a contract of marine insurance in India, codifying indemnity, insurable interest, utmost good faith and disclosure, warranties, the classes of loss, general average, sue and labour and subrogation
authority_sources.checked: Confirmed as at 24 August 2026 to be the current Indian statute governing contracts of marine insurance, and confirmed NOT to have been repealed by India's 2025 maritime legislation, which replaced the Merchant Shipping Act 1958 and the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1925 and did not touch the 1963 Act. The doctrines are named at the level the question needs; MIW has NOT read the Gazette text for this entry and therefore quotes no section numbers, which is declared in the study guide rather than left to look like an omission.

authority_sources.source: Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 2025 (Act 19 of 2025) and the Bills of Lading Act, 2025 (Act 18 of 2025) - the Indian carriage regime and the transfer of rights under a bill of lading; both in force from 10 September 2025 vide S.O. 4082(E) and S.O. 4083(E) of 8 September 2025, repealing the Indian Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1925 and the Indian Bills of Lading Act 1856 respectively
authority_sources.checked: Established at source, and NOT from a secondary summary. Both Acts were read in the official Gazette of India - including the entire Schedule to Act 19 of 2025 - during MIW's verification of the solved paper QP2510 Q2, whose record carries the Gazette references and the commencement notifications. Two facts recovered from that reading changed this entry and are the reason it does not read like a textbook: FIRST, commencement is established as 10 September 2025, so there is no open question about which statute book governs. SECOND, the Schedule enacts the Hague Rules as amended WITH MODIFICATIONS and departs from Hague-Visby in four respects - 'goods' includes live animals and deck cargo, the one-year time bar is extendable by three months by the court, Article IV bis is absent, and the limitation is 666.67 units of account per package or unit or 2 per kilogramme, whichever is higher. An answer built on 'Hague-Visby' generically would have carried the deck-cargo EXCLUSION into an Indian answer where the opposite is true, so this was the single most valuable check performed on this entry. No rupee conversion of the unit of account is asserted.

authority_sources.source: Compulsory insurance and financial security under the liability conventions - CLC 1992, the Bunkers Convention 2001, the Nairobi Wreck Removal Convention 2007, the Athens Convention as amended by the 2002 Protocol, and MLC 2006 financial security for repatriation and for death or long-term disability
authority_sources.checked: Cited for one proposition only and confirmed in force as at 24 August 2026: that each of these regimes requires evidence of insurance or other financial security to be maintained and carried. No monetary limit is quoted from any of them, because those limits are expressed in units of account and are periodically raised, and a stale figure would be a false statement about current law.

authority_sources.source: York-Antwerp Rules 2016 (Comite Maritime International, adopted 6 May 2016) - the private codification under which general average is adjusted
authority_sources.checked: Labelled honestly rather than conveniently. The York-Antwerp Rules are NOT an instrument of any of the accepted primary classes: they are a private, voluntary codification which binds only because contracts of carriage and policies incorporate them, and the edition that applies is the edition the contract names. That is why the answer refers to them by name for the mechanism of adjustment and does not cite a rule number or state which edition governs a given adventure. The 2016 edition, adopted at the CMI conference in New York on 6 May 2016, is the current edition and is the one most modern contracts incorporate; older editions remain in force wherever a contract still names one, and MIW's own solved papers correctly answer the 1994 edition where an examiner printed it.

authority_sources.source: Market policy wordings - Institute Time Clauses Hulls and the International Hull Clauses 2003 for hull and machinery; Institute Cargo Clauses (A), (B) and (C) for cargo
authority_sources.checked: Named as MARKET documents rather than law, which is the honest classification and is also the exam-correct one. The answer uses them only for structure - agreed value, deductible, the named heads of claim, all-risks against named-perils cover, and the three-fourths collision proportion under the traditional running down clause - and quotes no clause numbers or wording, because the clause set actually incorporated is a matter of the individual contract.

superseded_framework: Indian Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1925 (as amended in 1993) and the Indian Bills of Lading Act 1856 - both repealed with effect from 10 September 2025 by the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 2025 and the Bills of Lading Act 2025 respectively. Named here so that nobody restores them: they appear in older answer material and in almost every published note on this subject, and they must not be cited as present-day Indian law. MIW's own solved answers correctly cite them for sittings BEFORE that date, which is sitting-anchoring working as intended and is not a contradiction of this entry.

The proposition that 'goods' exclude live animals and deck cargo - true of Hague-Visby, and true of Indian law before 10 September 2025 - is FALSE under the Schedule to the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 2025, which includes both.

review_record.notes: Reviewed against the question and the cited authority. FIVE checks, and the second is the one that decided the verdict. SCOPE: the question has three parts and the answer has four headed sections mapping onto them, with the third part - documents and validity - given a full table rather than a list. That is the correct weighting, because it is the part the printed wording specifically asks for and the part most published notes on this topic omit. ACCURACY, and this is where a marine insurance answer usually fails: the hull/cargo boundary is drawn correctly and explicitly - cargo damage reaches the shipowner as a bill-of-lading liability met by P&I, not by the hull policy - and general average is distinguished from particular average by the DELIBERATE nature of the sacrifice rather than by size. Collision liability is correctly split, with the excluded heads named. Sue and labour is correctly described as payable in addition to the loss. CURRENTNESS was the real work, and the finding is a genuine correction to what this subject is normally taught from: the Indian carriage statute is no longer the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1925 but the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 2025, and the repealed Act is listed under superseded_framework precisely so that it is not quietly reinstated by the next reviewer. The Marine Insurance Act 1963 was separately confirmed NOT to have been swept up in the same reform. NUMBERS: only four are given, each of them structural rather than tariff - one year, three-fourths, five years, and the assent date - and the entry declines to quote convention limitation amounts or Act section numbers, saying in terms why. That is the right call: a stale SDR figure would be a false statement about current law, and this answer contains none. AUTHORITY HONESTY: the York-Antwerp Rules and the Institute clauses are labelled ENGINEERING_JUDGEMENT rather than being dressed as primary instruments, with an explicit statement that they bind only through incorporation. That is uncomfortable-looking and it is correct - they are not IMO instruments, not treaties and not statutes, and the accepted vocabulary has no better home for a private codification. The alternative would have been to inflate them into a primary class, which is exactly the failure this layer exists to prevent. EXAM UTILITY: the answer tells a candidate the three things that actually decide claims on a ship - survey before repair, split the yard account, keep class alive - and names the time bars. PASS. CORRECTED DURING REVIEW, and this is the finding worth recording. The entry as first drafted said MIW had not established the commencement of the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 2025 and relied on 'the Hague-Visby content common to both' regimes. Both statements were wrong against MIW's OWN corpus, which had already read both 2025 Acts in the Gazette of India during the verification of QP2510 Q2: commencement is 10 September 2025, and the Schedule departs from Hague-Visby in four respects. The second error was the dangerous one - a generic Hague-Visby answer states that deck cargo and live animals are outside the rules, and under the Indian Schedule they are inside it. The entry now states the Indian position from the Indian text. The lesson is the reuse rule applied to AUTHORITY rather than to answers: before declaring a fact unestablished, check whether the corpus has already established it.

version_history.reason: First publication under QI Phase-2 tranche 003. QIF-EM-0080 is the highest-ranked NEW_MODERN_ANSWER_REQUIRED family in the corpus and MIW held no answer to it. Four solved candidates were read in full and all four were rejected as owners: they answer the types of policy and their exclusions, P&I against H&M, the running down clause with general average expenses, and general average itself - and not one of them states the documents and information required from the ship or their validity, which is a third of this question. Corrected before publication against MIW's own primary reading of the two 2025 Indian Acts recorded in QP2510 Q2: commencement 10 September 2025, and four departures of the Indian Schedule from Hague-Visby, including the inclusion of live animals and deck cargo in 'goods'.
version_history.authority: Marine Insurance Act 1963 as the current Indian statute; Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 2025 (Act 19 of 2025) and Bills of Lading Act 2025 (Act 18 of 2025), both in force 10 September 2025 and read at source in the Gazette of India in MIW's QP2510 Q2 verification; the liability conventions for compulsory financial security; York-Antwerp Rules 2016 and the Institute / International Hull Clauses named as market and private-codification documents.

next_review_trigger: Re-review if (a) the Marine Insurance Act 1963 is amended or replaced - it is the one instrument behind this entry that has not been recently reformed and is therefore the one most likely to move next; (b) the Schedule to the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 2025 or the Bills of Lading Act 2025 is amended; (c) a limitation amount under any of the cited liability conventions is raised, which would matter only if a convention figure were ever added to this answer; or (d) MIW solves a past paper that sets the documents-and-validity task directly, in which case the relationship between that sitting-anchored answer and this one must be adjudicated rather than assumed. Routine re-review at twenty-four months: the Indian statute book was rebuilt in 2025 and is unlikely to move again soon, and the market wordings move slowly.
